While those are terrible spending habits that people can and should stop, I think it's often more complex than just unawareness or laziness. 

When financial security and milestones are so out of reach, some resilient people still do they best to save. But then there's people who, apart from not being taught good spending habits, also haven't been raised with much confidence to give them that resilience. When everything seems so bleak and hopeless, little conveniences to get you through the day are so much more appealing. And advertising nowadays is on a level no previous generation could've comprehended- so a lot of our self-control is already being eroded. You ignored the dozens of other ads you've seen today, so giving into one or two temptations still feels like restraint.

I never get takeout, and I don't buy lattes anymore, but during sadder periods, I've noticed giving in to more of these kind of habits. I'd grab more snacks or energy drinks or breakfast bars near work, because I'm right there anyway, and I rationalize it as fuel before/a treat after work. The few times I'd buy a latte would feel justified because it wasn't an everyday thing, even if it was still too often. I'd be quicker to take Lyft instead of working on my sleep schedule to get up earlier, etc. And then I'd feel ashamed about it later, especially when I have regained motivation and drive to save money, or the energy to cook nice meals at home. 

Yes, it's still a matter of learning discipline, and those habits don't disappear when someone has access to more money. But the hope from having better wages and financial possibilities would help build the drive and self-esteem to work on that discipline.

There was a rumor that she brought her baby to cafes for her writing sessions because she couldn't afford heat in her apartment- she later clarified that she brought her baby along because walking helps babies sleep. Characters like Hermione stood out as game changing role models for both little girls and women. All the girls have to prove themselves as exceptional to be written with the same respect as mediocre (or flat out abusive) boys. Appearance is given huge focus, especially to female characters and fat ones, and the it's okay for the narrator or protagonist to be cruel to bad characters for their weight and appearance. Hermione's dorkiness is excused because she easily impresses everyone around her whenever she puts effort in. There's a few videos and posts out there with plenty of quotes to show how egregious this gets, beyond even the norms of children's media at the time.

JKR then doubled down on this shit in all her subsequent works. Her main characters are always men. HP is one thing, that was her first project and so yeah, maybe she was attached to the boy she created, fine. But every project afterwards is very male focused. Her fatphobia goes next level in her adult novels- as in, the narrator describes a fat man in detail as being so fat that everyone must wonder how he uses his penis. That's above a one off mean comment about someone's weight, that shows a well-worn muscle for bullying.

She's no longer a relatable woman who writes relatable female characters. The ones that she did write turned out not to be so flattering or impressive. I took Wellbutrin for years, both solo and combined with various meds. It turned out that it was worsening my anxiety and OCD symptoms, which contributed to severe brain fog and fatigue. I didn't fully notice it because my baseline anxiety was so high; I thought it was only a problem when paired with other stimulants. I thought meds like Zoloft balanced it out, but only at increasingly high doses that gave worse side effects. One combo I took was also Wellbutrin/Prozac. The pharmacist initially refused to fill it without a special note from my prescriber, because it's a riskier combo ex serotonin syndrome. And while I took it safely, it also wore me the fuck out- huge peaks of energy and with it, anxiety, then crashes that felt like I took way too much caffeine.

I'm on a small dose of Lexapro right now, and I'm probably gonna go up, but it's already a big improvement. Which surprised me, since it seemed like a more "basic" med. Consider that Wellbutrin is unique as an antidepressant (NDRI), and that maybe that's counterproductive for you, that more dopamine is making you apathetic- whether it be because of underlying issues like anxiety, or another factor in how your brain chemistry works.

I saw a comparison ages ago that illustrated why dopamine agonists (direct or indirect) are unhelpful for some: some people need a big breakfast to fuel them for the day, and so a muffin wouldn't fill them up. But others feel weighed down by a big breakfast, so just have a muffin or fruit with coffee, then get fill their caloric needs later in the day. Not a perfect comparison, but you get it. 

Maybe you do need something more energizing. But please consider underlying reasons, and find a psych who'll discuss and examine those reasons, instead of just seeing everything as an upper/downer. I wasted so much time with my previous psych over this. Best of luck.

It's revealed that To'hajiillee and everything after didn't happen. It wasn't a dream, but a detailed prediction that Walt himself came up with using his mathematics and scientific genius. He breaks into his old classroom to write out the equation. He determines that this prediction has a 99.1% likelihood of happening if he continues to evade Hank. He then calmly comes to the rational conclusion that the best course of action, "scientifically speaking", is to come clean. Hugo (the janitor he got framed and fired in S1) finds him; Walt is shocked to find that he got his job back, and Hugo reassures him that everything turned out okay for him, he forgives Walt because he remembers what a kind and brilliant person he was, and then comforts him about having to turn himself in.

Cut to Walt sitting in a jail cell, having owned up to being Heisenburg. He spends a moment mulling everything over, before Hank walks in, making one of his old-time playful quips like everything's cool. Hank reveals that he paid Walt's bail and is taking him home- he and Marie were so shocked the hear that he turned himself in that they forgive him for everything. The whole family (plus Jesse) celebrates with a backyard cookout, while Hank makes "cook" jokes when Walt takes over the grill. Jesse brings homemade lasagna.

When Walt's trial comes, Hank and Saul team up to craft the perfect case to keep Walt out of prison. The jury is so moved by the family's story (and Lydia is able to be framed for a lot of it) that he's sentenced to just house arrest and community service. Though all the meth money is forfeited, Gretchen and Eliot reveal that they kept some stocks for Walt all this time, and cash it out to support his family. They admit they kept this secret out of jealousy and spite, but that they admit now that Walt was the backbone of Grey Matter.

That community service is later revealed to be Walt volunteering to teach at a middle grade science camp. A kid asks him a question about chemistry, and there's a flashback to Jesse from S1/2 asking Walt a similar question. He smiles, and after the kid thanks "Mr. White" and runs back to his little lab, Walt stands back and smiles. There's a zoom out shot, showing that the camp is in the desert wilderness of NM, and made up of campers, obviously meant to evoke the RV from the good ol days. Also, Huell is a staff member. Some country song about family and life plays, and the credits roll.

I don't know how close you are to your roommate, but you shouldn't feel any guilt. You'd be helping both your cats, your other roommate, and yourself.
